questions.stem: A student observes that a solution containing iron(II) ions is pale green, while a solution containing iron(III) ions is orange-brown. What property of transition metals does this demonstrate?

options.text: Transition metals have high melting points
Transition metals can form ions with different charges, producing differently coloured compounds
Transition metals are good conductors of electricity
Transition metals have high densities

questions.explanation: Transition metals can form ions with different charges (variable oxidation states). Iron can form Fe²⁺ (iron(II), pale green) and Fe³⁺ (iron(III), orange-brown). Each ion produces a different colour in solution, which is one of the distinctive properties of transition metals.

questions.stem: In the Haber process, iron is used as a catalyst. A factory manager asks why they cannot replace the iron with sodium, which is cheaper to produce. What is the best response?

options.text: Sodium could work but it is too expensive
Sodium is a Group 1 metal that would react violently with the reactants; only transition metals like iron can act as stable catalysts
Sodium has too high a melting point to be used as a catalyst
Sodium cannot be used because it is a gas at the temperatures used

questions.explanation: Transition metals make good catalysts because they can change oxidation state, providing a surface for reactions without being permanently changed. Sodium is a highly reactive alkali metal that would react with the nitrogen and hydrogen rather than catalysing their reaction. This ability to act as catalysts is a key property unique to transition metals.

questions.stem: Copper is used for water pipes and electrical wiring, while sodium must be stored under oil. Why is copper suitable for these everyday uses when sodium is not?

options.text: Copper is cheaper than sodium
Copper is much less reactive than sodium, has higher strength and melting point, and is an excellent conductor
Sodium is a non-metal and cannot conduct electricity
Copper is lighter than sodium

questions.explanation: Transition metals like copper are much less reactive than alkali metals like sodium. Copper does not react with water or air at room temperature, making it ideal for pipes and wiring. It also has a high melting point (1085°C), good strength, and excellent electrical conductivity — typical properties of transition metals.

questions.stem: A forensic scientist tests an unknown solution and finds it produces a blue precipitate when sodium hydroxide solution is added. Which ion is likely present?

options.text: Iron(II) ions, which form a green precipitate
Iron(III) ions, which form a brown precipitate
Copper(II) ions, which form a blue precipitate
Sodium ions, which form a white precipitate

questions.explanation: Adding sodium hydroxide to a solution containing copper(II) ions produces a blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide: Cu²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Cu(OH)₂. This is a standard test for identifying transition metal ions. Iron(II) gives green, iron(III) gives brown, and sodium ions do not form precipitates with NaOH.

questions.stem: Compared to Group 1 metals, transition metals generally have higher melting points, higher densities, and are harder. Which structural feature best explains these differences?

options.text: Transition metals have fewer protons in their nuclei
Transition metals have larger atomic radii
Transition metals have stronger metallic bonding due to more delocalised electrons from their inner electron shells
Transition metals have weaker intermolecular forces

questions.explanation: Transition metals have more electrons available for delocalisation compared to Group 1 metals (which contribute only 1 electron each). More delocalised electrons create stronger metallic bonds, resulting in higher melting points, greater hardness, and higher densities. This is why transition metals are commonly used as structural materials.
